passage: The lunch bell rang, and forty children poured into the narrow corridor outside Class 4B. Advait was squeezed against the wall when Gopika's elbow hit his shoulder and his water bottle clattered to the floor. "She did that on purpose," he told Sangeeta Ma'am, rubbing his arm. "She's always like that." Ten minutes later, racing back for his forgotten tiffin, Advait crashed straight into a Class 2 boy, who stumbled. "It wasn't my fault," Advait said quickly. "It's too crowded, and I was in a hurry." Sangeeta Ma'am raised an eyebrow. "So when you bump someone, it's the corridor. When Gopika bumps you, it's Gopika?" Advait opened his mouth, then closed it.

qa.q: What happened to Advait's water bottle?
qa.a: His water bottle clattered to the floor when Gopika's elbow hit his shoulder.

qa.q: Why does it feel true to Advait that Gopika did it on purpose?
qa.a: His arm hurts and he only feels the bump, not the forty children pushing Gopika, so meanness seems the obvious reason.

qa.q: What could Advait ask himself the next time someone bumps him?
qa.a: He could ask, 'Was it crowded, like when I bumped the Class 2 boy?' before deciding the person meant it.

qa.q: How might the Class 2 boy see Advait's excuse?
qa.a: The Class 2 boy only felt himself stumble, so he might think Advait was rough, just as Advait thought about Gopika.

grounding: A boy blames a classmate's nature for a bump in a packed corridor but blames the crowd when he bumps someone himself.

passage: I'm Vandana, Nakul's didi, and I ride the school bus with him. Yesterday the bus braked hard near the flyover and Madhuri, from his class, fell against him. His juice box squashed all over his shorts. "Madhuri is so rude," he announced to the whole back row. "She pushes everyone." I didn't see her push anyone; half the bus lurched forward. This morning, the same thing: brakes, lurch, and Nakul fell onto a Class 6 boy's lap. "The driver did it!" he said, laughing. I can't know what he was really thinking. But I noticed that when he fell, it was the bus, and when Madhuri fell, it was Madhuri.

qa.q: Where did the bus brake hard yesterday?
qa.a: The bus braked hard near the flyover.

qa.q: Why might Nakul feel so sure that Madhuri is rude?
qa.a: His juice squashed all over his shorts, so it may have felt personal to him, even though half the bus lurched.

qa.q: How could Vandana help Nakul see both falls the same way?
qa.a: Vandana could remind him of his own fall this morning and ask whether Madhuri might have been thrown by the brakes too.

qa.q: What is it like for Madhuri to be called rude in front of the back row?
qa.a: Madhuri may feel embarrassed and unfairly blamed for something the brakes caused.

grounding: An older sister notices her brother blaming a classmate's character for a bus bump while blaming the driver for his own.

passage:
Tuesday. In the crowded line for the drinking tap, Hafsa jostled Nitin and his shirt got soaked. "You did that on purpose," he snapped. At home he told Mummy that Hafsa was the meanest girl in Class 5.
Thursday. Nitin was carrying chart paper up the packed stairwell after assembly and knocked Hafsa's glasses clean off her face. "Sorry! The stairs were full," he said, and felt that was completely fair.
The next Monday. Miss Grace asked the class to draw the tap line as a bird would see it. Nitin drew thirty tiny heads squeezed together, with one small figure at the front being pushed. He looked at his drawing for a long time, then quietly said to Hafsa, "Maybe the line pushed you too."

qa.q: What did Nitin knock off Hafsa's face on Thursday?
qa.a: He knocked Hafsa's glasses clean off her face.

qa.q: Why did Nitin feel his own bump on the stairs was completely fair?
qa.a: Nitin felt no guilt because he knew the stairs were full and his arms were full of chart paper. His own reasons were clear to him in a way Hafsa's weren't.

qa.q: Which step helped Nitin see the tap line differently?
qa.a: Drawing the line from above showed thirty heads squeezed together, so the crowd became visible, not just Hafsa.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel when Nitin says, 'Maybe the line pushed you too'?
qa.a: Hafsa may feel relieved that he finally sees it wasn't meanness, especially after he knocked her glasses off himself. 🙂

grounding: Over several days a boy blames a girl's character for a bump, excuses his own by the crowd, and slowly notices the situation.

passage:
Faiz, you came home saying that boy pushed you on purpose? Let your Irfan Nana tell you about a corridor in 1968.
I was nine, in a small school in Lucknow. When the bell rang, all of us rushed through one narrow door to the tap. Someone slammed into me and my tiffin fell. It was Abhinav, a quiet boy from the back row. I shouted, "You're mean! You did it on purpose!" and told everyone he was a bully.
The very next day, the same bell, the same crowd, and I knocked a small girl's slate right out of her hands. She cried. And do you know what I said? "It's not my fault, it was too crowded!"
My Ammi heard both stories at home. She only asked, "Was the corridor also crowded yesterday?"

qa.q: What fell when someone slammed into Irfan in the corridor?
qa.a: His tiffin fell.

qa.q: Why did Irfan feel so sure Abhinav had pushed him on purpose?
qa.a: When he was the one knocked over, the pain and the fallen tiffin made it feel personal, so he explained it by Abhinav being mean rather than by the crowd.

qa.q: What could Faiz ask next time before deciding a push was on purpose?
qa.a: Faiz could ask what else was going on, like how crowded the place was, the same way Irfan Nana's Ammi asked about the corridor.

qa.q: How might Abhinav have felt being called a bully in front of everyone?
qa.a: Abhinav, a quiet boy, may have felt embarrassed and unfairly judged, since the push came from the rushing crowd, not from wanting to hurt anyone.

grounding: An elder recalls a boyhood day when he blamed a bumping classmate's character but excused his own bump the next day because of the crowd.

passage:
The lights went out halfway through Pema's birthday party, and twelve children in the small flat stumbled around in the dark while her mother searched for candles. Varun, eight, was holding a full cup of mango juice when someone crashed into him. Juice soaked his new shirt.
When the candles came on, Pema was standing right next to him.
"You did it! You're so mean," he shouted. He sat in the corner with his arms folded and wouldn't eat any cake.
Ten minutes later, the lights went out again. Varun jumped up to find the torch and stepped hard on a little boy's foot. The boy began to cry.
"It's not my fault," Varun said at once. "It's dark! Nobody can see anything!"
Pema's mother lit the candles again and looked at Varun for a moment. He looked at Pema, then at the floor.

qa.q: What happened to Varun's new shirt?
qa.a: Juice soaked his new shirt.

qa.q: Why did Varun feel sure Pema was mean but that his own bump was not his fault?
qa.a: When he got hurt, it felt like someone did it to him, so he blamed Pema, but when he bumped someone he could feel how dark it was, so the situation seemed to explain it.

qa.q: What could help Varun at this turning point, when he looked at the floor?
qa.a: An adult could quietly ask whether Pema's bump might also have been because of the dark, so Varun can reach the connection himself.

qa.q: How might Pema feel about being called mean at her own birthday party?
qa.a: Pema would likely feel hurt and confused, since the flat was dark and full and her party was spoilt by being blamed for an accident.

grounding: It shows a boy who is bumped in the dark calling the other child mean, then excusing his own bump the same evening because it was dark.

passage:
Monday
Today in the lunch line Wasim bumped me so hard my dal spilled on my shoe. He didn't even say sorry. He is SO mean. I told Rinku he does it on purpose because he thinks he's the boss of Class 4.
After lunch the bell rang and everyone ran for the stairs. I was squashed between big kids and I stepped on a little girl's foot. She cried. I said "sorry, it was crowded!" and ran. It WAS crowded.
Now I'm lying in bed thinking. The lunch line was crowded too. Wasim was holding his tray with both hands.
Maybe he's not mean. Maybe it was just the line.
Ramesh

qa.a: It spilled on Ramesh's shoe.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh think Wasim bumped on purpose?
qa.a: Ramesh felt angry and embarrassed about the spilled dal, so it seemed Wasim must be mean, without thinking about the crowded line.

qa.q: What question could Ramesh ask the next time someone bumps into him?
qa.a: Was it crowded or rushed, the way the stairs were when Ramesh stepped on the girl's foot?

qa.q: How might the little girl on the stairs see Ramesh?
qa.a: She might think Ramesh was mean or careless, the same way Ramesh judged Wasim.

grounding: A child's diary shows blaming a classmate's character for a bump while excusing their own bump as the crowd's fault.

passage: The morning bus to the taluk school was so packed that boys hung from the door rail. When it stopped at Chetan's village, Minakshi from the next lane shoved past him, and his tiffin box fell in the dust. "Rude!" Chetan shouted after her. "She thinks she owns the bus." He brushed off the box, fuming, and squeezed in last. At the next stop the bus braked suddenly, and Chetan fell against an old man with a basket of brinjals. "Sorry, Dadaji! The driver braked," he said, cheeks red. The old man nodded. "It's a crowded bus, beta." Chetan looked down the aisle at Minakshi, squashed between two women with bundles, her own bag held over her head.

qa.q: What happened to Chetan's tiffin box?
qa.a: It fell in the dust.

qa.q: Why did Chetan decide Minakshi was rude?
qa.a: He felt angry and embarrassed when his tiffin fell, so her character, not the packed bus, seemed to be to blame.

qa.q: What could Chetan remember the next time he is pushed on the bus?
qa.a: That the bus is crowded for everyone, just as it was when he fell against the old man, so a push may not mean someone is rude.

qa.q: How does the old man see Chetan bumping into him?
qa.a: The old man sees it as the crowded bus, not a rude boy, and calmly accepts the apology.

grounding: A boy calls a girl rude for pushing past on a packed bus, then excuses his own bump as the driver's braking.

passage: On the school skating day at the outdoor rink in Oslo, Xin was gliding slowly near the edge when Lars crashed into him and they both went down. "You did that on purpose!" Xin shouted. "You're always showing off." Lars, red-faced, said the ice was bumpy there, but Xin didn't listen. He told his friends Lars was a bully. Twenty minutes later, Xin hit the same bumpy patch, lost his balance and knocked over a smaller girl. "Sorry! The ice is terrible here!" he said, helping her up. On the bus home, rubbing his elbow, Xin remembered Lars saying almost exactly those words. He looked across at Lars, who was quietly picking ice out of his gloves.

qa.q: What did Lars say about the ice?
qa.a: That it was bumpy there.

qa.q: Why did Xin call Lars a bully?
qa.a: He felt hurt and angry after falling, so it seemed Lars must be showing off, even though Lars mentioned the bumpy ice.

qa.q: What could Xin do after noticing his own fall?
qa.a: Give Lars the same fair reading he gave himself, and perhaps apologise for calling him a bully.

qa.q: How might Lars feel being called a bully after an accident?
qa.a: Lars probably felt embarrassed and unfairly judged, since he explained about the ice and wasn't believed.

grounding: A boy blames another child's character for a crash on the ice, then blames the ice when he causes the same kind of fall.

passage: The lunch bell rang and the corridor outside Class 3 filled in seconds. Suraj was carrying his water bottle with the lid open when Ramesh bumped into him. Water splashed all over Suraj's shirt. "You did that on purpose!" Suraj shouted. "Ramesh is mean. Everyone knows." Ramesh opened his mouth, but a wave of children pushed him away. Two minutes later, rushing to the canteen, Suraj knocked a small girl's tiffin out of her hands. "Sorry, sorry, it's so crowded!" he said, and kept going. The duty teacher had seen both. "Suraj, when you bumped her, why did it happen?" "Because of the crowd." "And when Ramesh bumped you?" Suraj stopped. He looked back at the corridor, packed from wall to wall.

qa.q: What did Suraj knock out of the small girl's hands?
qa.a: Her tiffin.

qa.q: Why did Suraj feel so sure Ramesh bumped him on purpose?
qa.a: Soaked and upset, Suraj felt angry and blamed Ramesh's character, without noticing the crowded corridor he later used as his own excuse.

qa.q: How did the duty teacher help Suraj see the pattern?
qa.a: The teacher asked the same question about both bumps, so Suraj could compare his reason for himself with his reason for Ramesh.

qa.q: What is it like for Ramesh to be called mean in front of everyone?
qa.a: Ramesh probably feels hurt and unfairly judged, and he couldn't even explain because the crowd pushed him away.

grounding: Shows a child calling another child mean for bumping him in a crowded corridor while excusing his own bump as the crowd's fault.

passage:
Monday. In the crush at the school-bus door, Leela stepped on Akash's new shoe. He glared all the way home and told Amma, "Leela is the rudest girl in the whole bus."
Wednesday. It rained, and everyone rushed for the bus at once. Akash, pushing to get a window seat, elbowed a younger boy into the door. The boy cried out. "It wasn't me, everyone was pushing!" Akash said.
Friday. Akash got on first for once and watched from the window. The queue was a tangle of umbrellas and bags. Leela was squeezed near the door, trying not to step on anyone, and still bumped a Class 2 boy. She looked so sorry. Akash thought about Monday. Maybe it hadn't been rude. Maybe it had just been the door.

qa.q: What did Leela step on at the school-bus door?
qa.a: Akash's new shoe.

qa.q: How did Akash feel about Leela after Monday?
qa.a: He felt angry and sure that she was simply rude, calling her the rudest girl in the whole bus.

qa.q: What could Akash do the next time someone bumps him?
qa.a: He could look at the situation first, like the crowded door, before deciding the person is rude.

qa.q: How might the younger boy Akash elbowed see Akash on Wednesday?
qa.a: The younger boy may think Akash is rough or mean, just as Akash had judged Leela.

grounding: Shows a child blaming a girl's character for a bump at a crowded bus door while excusing his own push as everyone pushing.

passage: Hrithik, stop sulking. You say that boy in your class shoved you because he's a bully? Let me tell you what happened to your Bhupen Dadu when I was about your size. It was the Rath Yatra fair in Puri, the crowd like a river. A boy in a yellow shirt knocked my sugar candy right into the mud. I decided he was the wickedest boy in Odisha. I told my mother and cousins. Then, ten minutes later, the crowd surged, and I fell against an old man and knocked his glasses off. I said, "It was the crowd, it wasn't me!" My mother just looked at me. "And the boy in yellow?" she asked. I had no answer. So, Hrithik, was the corridor crowded when he shoved you?

qa.q: What did the boy in the yellow shirt knock into the mud?
qa.a: Bhupen Dadu's sugar candy.

qa.q: What was young Bhupen feeling toward the boy in yellow?
qa.a: He felt angry and sure the boy was the wickedest boy in Odisha, judging his character instead of the crowd.

qa.q: Which moment in the story made young Bhupen rethink?
qa.a: When his mother asked "And the boy in yellow?" right after he blamed the crowd for knocking off the old man's glasses.

qa.q: How might the old man have seen young Bhupen's excuse?
qa.a: The old man might have accepted that the crowd was to blame, the same understanding Bhupen had refused the boy in yellow.

grounding: An elder recalls blaming a boy's character for a bump at a crowded fair while excusing his own bump as the crowd's fault.

passage:
It was the Christmas concert, and the corridor was packed. Nilesh was carrying his drum to the stage, already late. Suddenly Nikita bumped into him hard, and his drumstick fell.

"She's so mean!" he said to his friend. "She did it on purpose."

Five minutes later, Nilesh himself rushed past a Class 2 boy and knocked his paper crown off. "Sorry, sorry, it's so crowded!" he called, not stopping.

After the concert, Nikita came to find him. "I'm sorry I bumped you. Someone pushed me from behind."

Nilesh opened his mouth, then closed it. When he bumped someone, it was the crowd. When Nikita bumped him, it was because she was mean.

He picked up his drum. "It's okay. It was crowded," he said, and this time he meant it.

qa.q: What fell when Nikita bumped Nilesh?
qa.a: His drumstick fell.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh think Nikita bumped him on purpose?
qa.a: Nilesh felt angry and hurt, and read the bump as her being mean rather than the crowded corridor.

qa.q: What could Nilesh remember next time someone bumps him?
qa.a: Nilesh could remember that he bumped someone too because of the crowd, and think about the situation before deciding someone is mean.

qa.q: How might Nikita feel if she knew Nilesh called her mean?
qa.a: Nikita might feel hurt and misunderstood, since she was pushed and came to apologise.

grounding: On a busy concert day, a child decides a classmate who bumped him is mean, but excuses his own bump as the crowd.

passage:
The Diwali mela in the colony was packed. Hemant was queueing for the giant wheel when Anirban, a boy from his building, knocked into him. Hemant's sparkler dropped into a puddle.

"He's always pushing," Hemant said. "He's rude."

A little later, running to catch up with his cousin, Hemant stepped on a little girl's foot. She cried. "It wasn't my fault," he told his cousin. "It's so crowded here."

His cousin looked at him. "When Anirban bumps you, he's rude. When you step on someone, it's the crowd?"

Hemant went quiet.

Near the sweet stall, Anirban came up with a new sparkler. "Sorry about before. Someone pushed me into you."

Hemant took the sparkler. He thought about the little girl's foot. "It's okay. It's really crowded," he said.

qa.q: What happened to Hemant's sparkler?
qa.a: Hemant's sparkler dropped into a puddle.

qa.q: Why did Hemant call Anirban rude but excuse himself?
qa.a: Hemant felt annoyed at Anirban and read the bump as rudeness, while seeing his own mistake as caused by the crowd.

qa.q: What did Hemant's cousin say that helped?
qa.a: The cousin pointed out that Hemant blamed Anirban's character but blamed the crowd for himself.

qa.q: How might the little girl have felt when Hemant stepped on her foot?
qa.a: The little girl was hurt and upset, and may have thought Hemant was careless.

grounding: At a festival fair, a child decides a boy who bumped him is rude but excuses his own bump as the crowd.

passage:

"That was an accident! There was a big puddle and I couldn't stop."

"Hmm. So when you splash someone, it's the puddle. When he splashes you, he's mean?"

"How?"

Pranav looked at his wet shorts. "I don't know."

"Maybe he couldn't stop either."

"Maybe." He sighed. "Can I have a towel?"

qa.a: The boy may not have even noticed, or may have felt sorry but unable to stop in the puddles.

grounding: During the monsoon, a child decides a cyclist who splashed him is mean but excuses his own splash as the puddle.

passage: On the first rainy day of July, everyone crowded into the school corridor because the ground was a lake. I was holding my wet umbrella when Suraj banged into me and my tiffin fell open. "You're so mean!" I shouted. He said sorry, but I didn't listen. I told everyone Suraj was a bully. Ten minutes later I got squashed near the staircase, and my elbow hit a small girl from class two. She started crying. "It wasn't my fault," I told the teacher. "It's so crowded!" At home I told Mummy about both bumps. She raised her eyebrows. "Sumit, so which one of you is mean?" I didn't have an answer. I still don't, really.

qa.q: What happened to Sumit's tiffin?
qa.a: It fell open when Suraj banged into Sumit in the corridor.

qa.q: Why did Sumit call Suraj mean but say the second bump wasn't Sumit's fault?
qa.a: Sumit felt the crowd pushing during the second bump but only saw Suraj in the first, so being angry at Suraj felt fair while Sumit felt defensive about the second.

qa.q: What could Sumit ask the next time someone bumps into Sumit?
qa.a: Sumit could ask whether the crowd might have caused it, just like the squash by the staircase, before calling anyone mean.

qa.q: How might Suraj feel after being called a bully?
qa.a: Suraj probably feels hurt and unfairly judged, having said sorry for an accident in a packed corridor.

grounding: Shows a child calling a classmate mean for a bump in a crowded corridor while excusing a similar bump of their own because of the crowd.
